stem: An 18-month-old boy who has not received routine vaccines has had fever, irritability and vomiting for 2 days. He is lethargic with a stiff neck and a bulging fontanelle. A lumbar puncture shows a high opening pressure.
oneliner: 18M + unvaccinated + fever, vomiting, stiff neck, bulging fontanelle + high opening pressure → which CSF profile?
ask: Which cerebrospinal fluid profile is most likely?

options.A: Lymphocytes predominate, protein mildly raised, glucose normal
options.B: Lymphocytes predominate, protein very high, glucose low
options.C: No cells, protein high, glucose normal
options.D: Neutrophils predominate, protein high, glucose low
options.E: Normal cells, protein and glucose

whyNot.A: The **viral** pattern; an unvaccinated toddler this ill with high pressure points to bacteria
whyNot.B: The pattern of **TB or fungal** meningitis, which evolves over **weeks**, not 2 days
whyNot.C: **Albuminocytologic dissociation** of Guillain-Barré; this boy has meningeal signs, not weakness
whyNot.E: He has **meningitis signs and high pressure**; a normal CSF would not explain them

answer: Neutrophilic pleocytosis, raised protein and low glucose (bacterial meningitis)
why: Bacteria in the subarachnoid space attract **neutrophils** and break down the blood-CSF barrier, so **protein rises**. Bacteria and neutrophils **consume glucose**, so CSF glucose falls (below about 40% of serum). Opening pressure is **high**. Viral meningitis gives **lymphocytes with normal glucose**.

idea.rule: Bacterial = neutrophils, high protein, low glucose; viral = lymphocytes, normal glucose.
also: TB and fungal meningitis: lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose
Guillain-Barré: high protein with normal cell count
Likely organisms in the unvaccinated young child: S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae type b
Neonates: group B Streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria

stem: A 32-year-old woman with AIDS, not taking antiretroviral therapy, has had two weeks of headache and confusion. Her CD4 count is 38/mm3. MRI shows a single enhancing lesion next to the lateral ventricle. After two weeks of treatment for toxoplasmosis, the lesion has not shrunk and she is no better.
oneliner: 32F + AIDS, CD4 38 + headache, confusion + single periventricular enhancing mass + no response to anti-toxoplasma therapy → which CSF finding?
ask: Which CSF finding most strongly supports the diagnosis?

options.A: Positive cryptococcal antigen
options.B: JC virus DNA
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus DNA by PCR
options.D: Oligoclonal IgG bands
options.E: Positive VDRL

whyNot.A: **Cryptococcal antigen** diagnoses meningitis, which causes headache and raised pressure, not a solitary mass
whyNot.B: **JC virus DNA** gives progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, with non-enhancing white matter lesions
whyNot.D: **Oligoclonal bands** are typical for multiple sclerosis, which does not fit a solitary mass in advanced AIDS
whyNot.E: **VDRL** is positive in neurosyphilis, which causes meningovascular disease and not a solitary mass

answer: Epstein-Barr virus DNA in the CSF (primary CNS lymphoma)
why: A **solitary periventricular enhancing mass** in AIDS with CD4 below 50 that does **not respond to toxoplasmosis therapy** suggests **primary CNS lymphoma**. It is driven by **Epstein-Barr virus**, so **EBV DNA in the CSF** supports lymphoma over toxoplasmosis.

idea.rule: AIDS brain mass: ring-enhancing multiple = toxo; solitary, periventricular, EBV+ = lymphoma.
also: Toxoplasmosis: multiple ring-enhancing lesions
Lymphoma is a B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma
Biopsy is needed if no response
CD4 below 100 raises risk

stem: A 51-year-old woman has a sudden severe headache followed by double vision. She has no diabetes or hypertension. CT angiography shows a 6-mm aneurysm at the junction of the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries, pressing on the adjacent cranial nerve.
oneliner: 51F + thunderclap headache + double vision + PComm aneurysm → which eye finding?
ask: Which eye finding is most likely?

options.A: Ptosis, eye down and out, pupil large and unreactive
options.B: Ptosis, eye down and out, pupil normal size and reactive
options.C: Mild ptosis, eye straight, pupil small and reactive
options.D: No ptosis, eye turned inward, pupil normal
options.E: No ptosis, eye slightly raised, pupil normal

whyNot.B: Pupil sparing is typical of **microvascular** (diabetic, hypertensive) palsy; she has **neither**, and a compressing aneurysm squeezes the **superficial pupil fibers**
whyNot.C: This is **Horner syndrome**, a sympathetic lesion with a **small** pupil; a posterior communicating aneurysm compresses the nerve that **lifts the lid and moves the eye**, not the sympathetic chain
whyNot.D: An inward-turned eye is a **CN VI** palsy, and that nerve does not run beside this aneurysm
whyNot.E: A slightly raised eye with normal pupil is a **CN IV** palsy, which is not the nerve beside this aneurysm

answer: Ptosis, eye down and out, large unreactive pupil
why: A posterior communicating aneurysm compresses **CN III**. Loss of the levator gives **ptosis**, loss of the medial and vertical muscles leaves the eye **down and out** (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), and the **parasympathetic fibers on the surface** are hit first, so the pupil is **dilated and unreactive**.

idea.rule: A compressive CN III palsy involves the pupil early; an ischemic (diabetic) palsy usually spares it.
also: Uncal herniation compresses CN III against the tentorium
Midbrain lesions can cause CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber)
Cavernous sinus aneurysm can combine CN III with other nerves
Diabetic microvascular palsy: pupil-sparing

stem: A 57-year-old man has 8 months of progressive weakness in both hands with painful muscle cramps and an 8-kg weight loss. More recently his speech has become slurred and he chokes on thin liquids.
oneliner: 57M + progressive hand weakness + cramps + weight loss + slurred speech + choking → which examination findings?
ask: Which set of examination findings is most likely?

options.A: Wasting, absent reflexes, stocking-distribution sensory loss
options.B: Brisk reflexes with cape-like loss of pain and temperature
options.C: Wasting and fasciculations with brisk reflexes and intact sensation
options.D: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal reflexes
options.E: Ascending weakness, absent reflexes, loss of vibration sense

whyNot.A: A polyneuropathy is **length-dependent** and starts in the feet; his weakness began in the **hands** and spread to **speech and swallowing**
whyNot.B: A cervical syrinx wastes the hands but evolves over years and does not explain **cramps, 8-kg weight loss** and **slurred speech with choking** within 8 months
whyNot.D: Myasthenia fluctuates through the day; his weakness is **steadily progressive over 8 months** with cramps
whyNot.E: Guillain-Barre evolves over **days to weeks**, not 8 months

answer: Wasting and fasciculations with brisk reflexes, sensation intact
why: This is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: loss of **lower motor neurons** (wasting, fasciculations) and **upper motor neurons** (hyperreflexia, spasticity) in the same limbs and the bulbar region. **Sensation, eye movements and sphincters are spared.**

idea.rule: ALS is combined upper and lower motor neuron disease with sensory, ocular and bladder sparing.
also: Riluzole (glutamate release inhibitor) slows progression
SOD1 mutation causes familial ALS
Onuf nucleus is spared, so bladder function is preserved
Primary lateral sclerosis is upper motor neuron only
Spinal muscular atrophy is lower motor neuron only

stem: A 26-year-old woman has double vision and drooping eyelids that build through the day and clear after a night's rest, and her arms tire when she brushes her hair. Tendon reflexes are normal. Her symptoms improve after a trial of pyridostigmine, and repetitive stimulation of the ulnar nerve is performed.
oneliner: 26F + diplopia + evening ptosis + tiring arms + better on pyridostigmine → which electrodiagnostic result?
ask: Which electrodiagnostic result is most likely?

options.A: A small first response that grows over 100% with high-frequency stimulation
options.B: A progressive fall in response amplitude over the first few stimuli
options.C: Slowed conduction velocity with conduction block
options.D: Fibrillation potentials and fasciculations in several limbs
options.E: Myotonic discharges with delayed relaxation

whyNot.A: An incremental response is the **Lambert-Eaton** pattern, which brings **reduced reflexes**; her reflexes are **normal** and her **eye muscles** are most affected
whyNot.C: Slowed conduction suggests **demyelination**; her symptoms **fluctuate and respond to pyridostigmine**
whyNot.D: Denervation changes in several limbs would give **wasting and fixed weakness**, not fluctuation that eases with a cholinesterase inhibitor
whyNot.E: Myotonic discharges accompany **delayed muscle relaxation**, not fatigable ocular and arm weakness

answer: Decremental response with slow repetitive stimulation
why: Myasthenia gravis has **antibodies to the postsynaptic nicotinic receptor**, so safety factor at the junction is low. With repeated stimuli, acetylcholine release falls and fewer fibers reach threshold, giving a **decrementing compound muscle action potential**. Reflexes are preserved and pyridostigmine helps.

idea.rule: Myasthenia gravis shows decrement on slow repetitive nerve stimulation; Lambert-Eaton shows increment on fast stimulation.
also: Edrophonium or ice pack test improves ptosis
Thymoma or thymic hyperplasia often accompanies it
Anti-AChR antibodies are found in most patients
Lambert-Eaton syndrome: presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, small cell lung cancer

stem: A 29-year-old competitive cyclist has had 3 weeks of weak grip on the handlebars and keeps dropping his water bottle. The weakness began after he moved to a handlebar position that presses on the base of the palm on the little-finger side. He has no pain, and sensation in the hand is normal.
oneliner: 29M + cyclist + 3 weeks weak grip + pressure at the base of the palm → which motor finding?
ask: Which examination finding is most likely?

options.A: Weak thumb opposition with thenar wasting
options.B: Wrist drop with weak finger extension
options.C: Weak elbow flexion and forearm supination
options.D: Cannot flex the thumb and index fingertips to make an OK sign
options.E: Weak finger spreading and closing, with a positive Froment sign

whyNot.A: Thenar muscles are **median** nerve territory; the pressure is on the **little-finger side** of the palm
whyNot.B: The radial nerve runs on the **back of the arm and forearm**, away from palmar handlebar pressure
whyNot.C: Elbow flexion and supination come from muscles supplied by the **musculocutaneous nerve**, far from the **palm**
whyNot.D: This is an **anterior interosseous** (median) injury, which is not caused by pressure on the **base of the palm**

answer: Weak finger abduction and adduction with a positive Froment sign
why: Pressure over the **hook of the hamate** compresses the deep motor branch of the **ulnar nerve**. It weakens the **interossei** (finger abduction and adduction) and the adductor pollicis, so the flexor pollicis longus (median) substitutes in a paper pinch: a **Froment sign**.

idea.rule: Ulnar nerve motor loss: interossei, adductor pollicis and medial lumbricals; the deep branch spares sensation.
also: Cubital tunnel (elbow) injury adds numbness of the ring and small fingers
Claw hand follows low ulnar lesions
Hook of hamate fracture can injure the deep branch
Handlebar palsy is sometimes called cyclist's palsy

stem: A 72-year-old woman over 5 months has noticed her feet seem stuck to the floor when she starts to walk. She then developed urinary urgency with accidents and, more recently, forgetfulness. She has no headache, her fundi are normal and her behavior is unchanged. Head CT is obtained.
oneliner: 72F + gait trouble first + urinary incontinence + forgetfulness + no headache → which CT finding?
ask: Which head CT finding is most likely?

options.A: Ventricles and sulci equally widened
options.B: Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a small fourth ventricle
options.C: Slit-like ventricles with an empty sella
options.D: Ventricles enlarged out of proportion to the cortical sulci
options.E: A large frontal mass with surrounding edema

whyNot.A: Atrophy gives **memory loss first**; her **gait and bladder** problems came before the forgetfulness
whyNot.B: Aqueductal stenosis causes **raised pressure with headache and papilledema**, and she has **no headache and normal fundi**
whyNot.C: Slit ventricles with an empty sella point to **raised intracranial pressure** in a woman with **headache and papilledema**, which she lacks
whyNot.E: A frontal mass would produce **focal signs or raised pressure** (headache); her course is slow with gait and bladder symptoms

answer: Ventricles enlarged out of proportion to sulci
why: Gait disturbance, incontinence and cognitive slowing form the triad of **normal pressure hydrocephalus**, a communicating hydrocephalus from poor CSF absorption. CT shows **ventricular enlargement out of proportion to the sulci**, unlike atrophy where **both widen together** (ex vacuo).

idea.rule: Normal pressure hydrocephalus: ventricles larger than the sulci predict; atrophy enlarges both together.
also: Triad: wet, wobbly, wacky (urinary incontinence, magnetic gait, dementia)
Potentially reversible with CSF drainage or a shunt
Lumbar puncture opening pressure is normal
Alzheimer disease causes hydrocephalus ex vacuo

stem: A 4.4-kg newborn boy is delivered after prolonged shoulder dystocia, with traction on the head away from the shoulder. His mother notices less movement at the right shoulder and elbow than at the left. The right hand grasps strongly.
oneliner: Newborn M + 4.4 kg + shoulder dystocia + head traction + strong right grasp → which arm finding?
ask: Which arm finding is most likely?

options.A: Arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated
options.B: Clawed hand with absent grasp, and a small pupil with ptosis on that side
options.C: Hand flexed at the wrist and unable to extend, with normal shoulder and elbow movement
options.D: Entire arm limp with absent grasp and no movement at any joint
options.E: Medial scapular border lifted off the chest wall with otherwise normal arm movement

whyNot.B: Klumpke palsy (C8-T1) paralyzes the **hand** and gives Horner syndrome, but his **grasp is strong**
whyNot.C: Wrist drop alone is a **radial** lesion; he has reduced movement at the **shoulder and elbow**
whyNot.D: Total plexus injury would remove the **grasp** as well
whyNot.E: Winging comes from a long thoracic nerve lesion; his **shoulder and elbow** movement is reduced

answer: Waiter's tip posture (adducted, internally rotated, extended, pronated arm)
why: Stretching the neck away from the shoulder injures the **upper trunk (C5-C6)**. Loss of deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis leaves the arm **adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended and forearm pronated** (waiter's tip), with the biceps reflex lost and hand grasp preserved.

idea.rule: Erb palsy (C5-C6) gives the waiter's-tip arm with a preserved hand; Klumpke (C8-T1) spares the shoulder and paralyzes the hand.
also: Shoulder dystocia and macrosomia are risk factors
Adults: motorcycle accidents that force the head and shoulder apart
Klumpke palsy follows hyperabduction traction with Horner syndrome
Most infants recover spontaneously

stem: A 46-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of numbness in her left hand. Her strength is normal. MRI shows a small enhancing lesion in the right postcentral gyrus over the hand region.
oneliner: 46F + 3 weeks left hand numbness + right postcentral gyrus lesion → which sensory deficit?
ask: Which sensory examination result is most likely?

options.A: Cape-like loss of pain and temperature across both arms
options.B: Glove-and-stocking loss of every modality
options.C: Lost stereognosis and graphesthesia in the left hand, pain sense kept
options.D: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense below a spinal level
options.E: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature below a spinal level

whyNot.A: A cape pattern comes from a **central cord** syrinx; her lesion is in the **cortex** and the numbness is confined to one hand
whyNot.B: Glove-and-stocking loss follows a **length-dependent polyneuropathy**; her numbness is **one hand** with a **cortical** lesion
whyNot.D: Dorsal-column loss is **ipsilateral to a spinal lesion**; hers is a **cortical** lesion with **contralateral** symptoms
whyNot.E: Spinothalamic loss below a spinal level is a **cord** pattern; her MRI shows a **cortical** lesion

answer: Astereognosis, agraphesthesia and impaired two-point discrimination in the left hand
why: The **primary somatosensory cortex** receives the contralateral hand through the thalamus. A lesion there spoils **discriminative sensation** (stereognosis, graphesthesia, two-point discrimination, position sense), while **crude pain and temperature** are relatively spared because they reach other cortical and subcortical areas.

idea.rule: Cortical sensory loss is contralateral and affects fine discrimination more than crude touch, pain and temperature.
also: Astereognosis: cannot identify an object by touch
Agraphesthesia: cannot read a number traced on the skin
Thalamic (VPL) lesion causes contralateral loss of all modalities
The homunculus places the hand and face laterally (MCA) and the leg medially (ACA)

stem: A 16-year-old girl has had a generalized headache for several weeks. Several times a day her vision fades in one eye or the other for a few seconds, then returns. Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes and the pupils react briskly.
oneliner: 16F + headache + transient visual fading + normal acuity and pupils → which eye finding is expected?
ask: Which eye examination finding is most likely?

options.A: Pale optic discs with reduced acuity
options.B: Swollen optic discs with blurred margins
options.C: Pain on eye movement with an afferent pupillary defect
options.D: Pale retina with a cherry-red macula
options.E: Bitemporal visual field loss

whyNot.A: **Acuity is 20/20** and she has no sustained visual loss, so optic atrophy does not fit
whyNot.C: Optic neuritis is typically **unilateral with an afferent pupillary defect and reduced acuity**; her pupils are normal and acuity is 20/20
whyNot.D: Central retinal artery occlusion gives **sudden, persistent, painless** loss in one eye, not seconds-long episodes in either eye with a headache
whyNot.E: A chiasmal mass would not give **brief fading in either eye** and would not explain weeks of generalized headache

answer: Swollen optic discs with blurred margins (papilledema)
why: Raised intracranial pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath and swells the discs (**papilledema**), blurring their margins and enlarging the physiologic blind spot. **Acuity and pupils stay normal** early, and seconds-long **transient visual obscurations** are typical.

idea.rule: Papilledema from raised ICP: swollen discs, enlarged blind spot, normal acuity early.
also: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: obese young woman with headache and visual obscurations
Sixth nerve palsy can accompany raised ICP (false localizing sign)
Persistent papilledema eventually causes optic atrophy and peripheral field loss
Mass lesions and venous sinus thrombosis also raise ICP

stem: A 70-year-old man notices that sounds are muffled on the right and his right ear feels blocked. Otoscopy shows wax filling the right canal. He has no vertigo or tinnitus and no other neurologic signs. A 512-Hz tuning fork is placed on the forehead and then tested at each mastoid and ear.
oneliner: 70M + right ear blocked by wax + muffled hearing + tuning-fork tests → which pair of Weber and Rinne results?
ask: Which pair of tuning-fork results is expected?

options.A: Weber lateralizes to the left; Rinne shows air louder than bone on the right
options.B: Weber lateralizes to the left; Rinne shows bone louder than air on the right
options.C: Weber lateralizes to the right; Rinne shows air louder than bone on the right
options.D: Weber lateralizes to the right; Rinne shows bone louder than air on the right
options.E: Weber is midline; Rinne shows air louder than bone in both ears

whyNot.A: That combination is the **sensorineural** pattern, but his canal is **blocked by wax**, which is a conductive cause
whyNot.B: Weber to the left means the **right** ear has a sensorineural loss; with **wax in the right canal** the tone goes to the blocked side
whyNot.C: With a **blocked right canal** air conduction is poorer on the right, so Rinne cannot show air louder than bone there
whyNot.E: A normal result would not explain **muffled hearing with wax obstructing the right canal**

answer: Weber to the right; Rinne negative on the right
why: A canal blockage cuts **air conduction** in that ear while the cochlea is intact. Bone-conducted sound is no longer masked by room noise, so **Weber lateralizes to the deaf (blocked) ear** and **Rinne is negative (bone > air)** on that side.

idea.rule: Conductive hearing loss: Weber toward the affected ear, Rinne negative there.
also: Otitis media with effusion
Otosclerosis (stapes fixation)
Tympanic membrane perforation
Sensorineural loss does the opposite: Weber to the good ear, Rinne still air > bone

stem: A 22-year-old man fractures the neck of his right fibula in a football tackle. Afterward he trips over curbs because he cannot lift the front of his foot. The knee and hip are strong. He is examined below the knee.
oneliner: 22M + fibular neck fracture + trips over curbs + knee and hip strong → which set of strength, sensation and reflex findings?
ask: Which set of strength, sensory and reflex findings is expected?

options.A: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion, numb dorsal foot, ankle reflex intact
options.B: Weak plantar flexion and inversion, numb sole, absent ankle reflex
options.C: Weak knee extension, numb anterior thigh, absent patellar reflex
options.D: Weak dorsiflexion and hip abduction, numb dorsal foot, reflexes intact
options.E: Normal strength, numb lateral thigh, reflexes intact

whyNot.B: Plantar flexion, inversion and the ankle reflex belong to the **tibial nerve/S1**; he **cannot lift his foot**, the opposite movement
whyNot.C: His **knee is strong**, so a femoral nerve lesion is excluded
whyNot.D: Weak hip abduction would point to an **L5 root** lesion; his **hip is strong** and the injury is at the **fibular neck**
whyNot.E: He has a clear **motor deficit at the foot**, so a purely sensory thigh nerve does not fit

answer: Foot drop with weak eversion, dorsal foot numbness and preserved ankle jerk
why: The **common peroneal nerve** winds around the fibular neck. Its deep branch lifts the foot (**dorsiflexion**) and the superficial branch **everts** it and supplies the **dorsum of the foot**. Plantar flexion and the **ankle reflex** run through the tibial nerve and are spared.

idea.rule: Common peroneal injury at the fibular neck: foot drop and dorsal foot numbness; plantar flexion and ankle jerk intact.
also: Compression from leg casts, prolonged crossing of the legs or lithotomy positioning
Steppage gait with high-lifted knee
L5 radiculopathy also gives foot drop but adds weak inversion and hip abduction
Weak inversion points to the tibial nerve and L5, not the peroneal nerve alone

stem: A 58-year-old woman had a hysterectomy two days ago with prolonged retractor placement in the pelvis. She now cannot climb stairs because her right knee buckles. Her foot movements are normal.
oneliner: 58F + pelvic surgery + knee buckles on stairs → which motor/reflex/sensory finding?
ask: Which set of motor, reflex and sensory findings is expected?

options.A: Weak plantar flexion, no ankle reflex, numb sole and lateral foot
options.B: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion, normal reflexes, numb dorsal foot
options.C: Weak thigh adduction, normal reflexes, numb medial thigh
options.D: Weak hip abduction, normal reflexes, normal sensation
options.E: Weak knee extension, no patellar reflex, numb anterior thigh and medial leg

whyNot.A: Plantar flexion and the **ankle reflex** are tibial/S1; her **foot movements are normal** and the problem is **knee buckling**
whyNot.B: **Foot movements are normal**, which excludes a peroneal nerve lesion
whyNot.C: Obturator (adductor) weakness would not make the **knee buckle on stairs**
whyNot.D: Hip abductor (superior gluteal) weakness gives a Trendelenburg gait, not a **buckling knee**

answer: Quadriceps weakness, no patellar reflex, anterior thigh and medial leg numbness
why: The **femoral nerve** (L2-L4) supplies the quadriceps, so **knee extension fails** and the **patellar reflex is lost**. Its cutaneous branches cover the anterior thigh and, via the **saphenous nerve**, the medial leg. Retractor pressure or groin catheterization can injure it.

idea.rule: Femoral nerve injury: weak knee extension, absent patellar reflex, anterior thigh and medial leg numbness.
also: Retroperitoneal hematoma in anticoagulated patients
Diabetic amyotrophy
Hip flexion is also weak because the iliopsoas is partly femoral
Obturator injury instead weakens adduction

stem: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the front of the left armpit. He now has difficulty lifting objects toward his chest and turning his palm up. Shoulder abduction, wrist extension and hand grip are normal.
oneliner: 30M + stab wound front of armpit + weak elbow flexion and palm-up turning + shoulder abduction and hand normal → which deficit set?
ask: Which set of deficits is most likely?

options.A: Weak wrist and finger extension, numb dorsal hand
options.B: Weak shoulder abduction, numb lateral shoulder
options.C: Weak elbow flexion and supination, numb lateral forearm
options.D: Weak finger abduction, numb medial hand
options.E: Weak thumb opposition, numb lateral palm

whyNot.A: **Wrist extension is normal**, which excludes a radial nerve lesion
whyNot.B: **Shoulder abduction is normal**, which excludes the axillary nerve
whyNot.D: **Hand grip is normal**, so an ulnar nerve deficit does not fit
whyNot.E: **Hand grip is normal**, so a median nerve deficit in the hand does not fit

answer: Weak elbow flexion and supination with lateral forearm numbness
why: The **musculocutaneous nerve** supplies the biceps and brachialis, so **elbow flexion and supination** weaken and the **biceps reflex** falls. Its terminal branch, the **lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve**, carries sensation from the lateral forearm; the hand is spared.

idea.rule: Musculocutaneous nerve: elbow flexion and supination weak, lateral forearm numb, hand spared.
also: Coracobrachialis also lies in its territory
Injured by penetrating axillary wounds and occasionally by anterior shoulder dislocation
Supination is weakened, not lost, because the supinator (radial nerve) still works
Biceps reflex is C5-C6

stem: A 46-year-old right-handed carpenter has had months of hand numbness that wakes him at night and improves when he shakes the hand. He now has trouble opening jars. He has no neck pain, and his forearm is not affected.
oneliner: 46M + repetitive hand use + nocturnal numbness + trouble opening jars → which area of sensory loss?
ask: Which area of sensory loss is most likely?

options.A: Dorsal lateral hand and thumb
options.B: Palmar and dorsal medial hand
options.C: Lateral hand and lateral forearm
options.D: Medial hand and medial forearm
options.E: Palmar lateral digits, thenar skin spared

whyNot.A: Radial sensory loss is **dorsal** and gives no grip weakness; night numbness eased by **shaking the hand** with **trouble opening jars** points to the carpal tunnel
whyNot.B: An ulnar pattern affects the **medial** hand and would not weaken the thumb grip needed to **open jars**
whyNot.C: A C6 root lesion would extend into the **forearm** and usually come with neck pain; his forearm is normal
whyNot.D: A C8 root lesion spreads over the **medial forearm**, and he has no neck pain or forearm symptoms

answer: Palmar lateral three and a half digits, sparing the thenar eminence
why: Carpal tunnel compression of the **median nerve** under the flexor retinaculum numbs the **palmar thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger**. The **palmar cutaneous branch** leaves the nerve before the tunnel, so **thenar skin is spared**.

idea.rule: Carpal tunnel: median digital sensory loss with thenar skin spared.
also: Phalen and Tinel signs
Associated with pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis
Late thenar muscle wasting
Pronator syndrome compresses the median nerve proximally and also numbs the thenar skin

stem: A 45-year-old man felt a pull in his back while lifting a crate. Since then pain has run down the back of his right thigh and calf to the outer border of the foot. He has normal bladder and bowel function and no numbness between the legs.
oneliner: 45M + lifting injury + back pain down the back of the leg to the lateral foot → which reflex/strength/sensory finding set?
ask: Which set of reflex, strength and sensory findings is expected?

options.A: Weak great toe extension, numb dorsal foot, normal reflexes
options.B: Weak plantar flexion, absent ankle reflex, numb lateral foot
options.C: Weak knee extension, absent patellar reflex, numb medial leg
options.D: Saddle numbness, urinary retention, absent anal reflex
options.E: Weak hip flexion, numb anterior thigh, normal reflexes

whyNot.A: That is **L5**, whose pain runs down the lateral leg to the **dorsum** of the foot, not the outer border and sole
whyNot.C: Knee extension and patellar reflex are **L4**, with pain to the medial leg
whyNot.D: He has **normal bladder function and no perineal numbness**, which excludes cauda equina syndrome
whyNot.E: Hip flexion and the anterior thigh are **L2-L3**; his pain follows the back of the leg

answer: Plantar flexion weakness, absent ankle jerk, lateral foot numbness
why: The **S1 root** supplies the gastrocnemius-soleus and carries the **ankle reflex**, and its dermatome covers the **lateral foot and sole**. A posterolateral disc herniation at L5-S1 compresses it, giving **pain down the back of the leg** to the lateral foot.

idea.rule: S1 radiculopathy: ankle reflex lost, plantar flexion weak, lateral foot and sole numb.
also: L5-S1 disc herniation compresses S1
L5 radiculopathy: foot dorsiflexion and great toe extension weak, reflexes normal
L4 radiculopathy: weak knee extension, absent patellar reflex
Straight leg raise reproduces L5 and S1 radicular pain

stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg with a spared face, and loss of vibration and position sense in the left limbs. MRI shows a small infarct near the midline of the medulla. He is asked to stick out his tongue.
oneliner: 68M + left hemiparesis sparing the face + left proprioceptive loss + medullary infarct → which tongue finding?
ask: Which tongue finding is most likely?

options.A: Tongue deviates to the right on protrusion
options.B: Tongue deviates to the left on protrusion
options.C: Tongue midline with left-sided atrophy
options.D: Tongue midline with fasciculations on both sides
options.E: Loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds

whyNot.B: Left-sided weakness and sensory loss from a medullary infarct place the lesion in the **right** medulla; the tongue deviates **toward** the lesion
whyNot.C: His lesion is in the **right** medulla, and a one-sided hypoglossal lesion **deviates** the tongue rather than leaving it midline
whyNot.D: Bilateral fasciculations suggest **bilateral lower motor neuron disease**, but his infarct is **one-sided**
whyNot.E: Anterior taste travels with the **facial nerve** to the solitary nucleus, not the **medial** medulla

answer: Deviation toward the right
why: The medial medulla holds the **pyramid**, **medial lemniscus** and exiting **hypoglossal fibers**. A right-sided infarct gives **contralateral (left) hemiparesis sparing the face** and left proprioceptive loss, and weakens the **right genioglossus**, so the protruded tongue **points toward the lesion** (right).

idea.rule: Hypoglossal lesion: the tongue deviates toward the weak side, the side of the lesion.
also: Medial medullary syndrome: ipsilateral tongue weakness, contralateral hemiparesis and loss of proprioception
Anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla
Cortical (UMN) lesion makes the tongue point away from the lesion, toward the weak side of the body
A hypoglossal nucleus lesion adds tongue atrophy and fasciculations

stem: A 68-year-old man has two days of hoarseness and trouble swallowing. The gag reflex is reduced on the left, and he is asked to say "ah" while the soft palate is observed.
oneliner: 68M + hoarseness + dysphagia + reduced left gag + saying ah → which palate/uvula finding?
ask: Which palate or uvula finding is expected?

options.A: Uvula deviates to the left
options.B: Uvula stays midline as the palate rises evenly
options.C: Uvula deviates to the right
options.D: Neither side of the palate rises
options.E: Right side of the palate fails to rise

whyNot.A: The left palate fails to rise, so the uvula is **pulled toward the intact right side**, not toward the weak side
whyNot.B: Hoarseness, dysphagia and a **reduced left gag** mean the left palate is weak, so the rise cannot be even
whyNot.D: Failure of both sides would need **bilateral** lesions; only the **left gag** is reduced
whyNot.E: A right-sided weakness would reduce the **right** gag, but his reduced gag is on the **left**

answer: Uvula deviates away from the lesion (to the right)
why: The vagus nerve raises the soft palate and moves the vocal cords and pharyngeal muscles. On the **lesioned (left) side the palate does not elevate**, so the **uvula deviates toward the normal side, away from the lesion**. **Hoarseness and dysphagia** reflect the same nerve injury.

idea.rule: Vagus lesion: the uvula points away from the lesion, to the side of the working palate.
also: Lateral medullary syndrome damages the nucleus ambiguus
Gag reflex: CN IX afferent, CN X efferent
Recurrent laryngeal injury causes hoarseness without palate deviation
A nucleus ambiguus lesion gives the same uvula deviation

stem: A 66-year-old woman has a painful vesicular rash across the left forehead and scalp. The left cornea feels numb. Her facial movements are symmetric. A wisp of cotton is touched to each cornea in turn while the examiner watches both eyes.
oneliner: 66F + herpes zoster left forehead + numb left cornea + symmetric face → which corneal reflex pattern?
ask: Which pattern of blinking is expected?

options.A: Touching either cornea: only the right eye blinks
options.B: Touching the left cornea: both eyes blink. Touching the right cornea: neither blinks
options.C: Neither eye blinks whichever cornea is touched
options.D: Touching the left cornea: neither eye blinks. Touching the right cornea: both eyes blink
options.E: Both eyes blink normally from either side

whyNot.A: That pattern belongs to a **left facial nerve** (efferent) lesion, but her **facial movements are symmetric**
whyNot.B: That is the **reverse** pattern, which would need a lesion of the **right** afferent limb; her **left** cornea is the numb one
whyNot.C: Both sides failing would need bilateral lesions; her **right cornea is intact**
whyNot.E: She has a **numb left cornea**, so the response cannot be normal

answer: Left side stimulation: no blink in either eye; right side stimulation: both blink
why: The corneal reflex has an **afferent limb in V1** (nasociliary) and an **efferent limb in the facial nerve**. With a **V1 lesion**, stimulating the affected cornea sends no signal, so **neither eye blinks**; the intact cornea still drives **both facial nerves**, so both eyes blink.

idea.rule: Afferent (V1) lesion: stimulating the affected side gives no blink at all; efferent (VII) lesion: the affected eye never blinks.
also: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus risks keratitis and uveitis
Hutchinson sign: vesicles on the nasal tip mean nasociliary (V1) involvement and eye risk
Facial nerve palsy: the affected eye cannot blink, but the other eye blinks to either side
The spinal trigeminal nucleus projects to both facial nuclei, so one cornea drives both blinks

stem: A 64-year-old man develops sudden vertigo, nausea and unsteadiness. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation over the right face and the left half of the body, and clumsiness of the right arm and leg. Strength is full.
oneliner: 64M + vertigo + crossed pain-temperature loss + right limb ataxia → which additional finding is expected?
ask: Which additional finding is expected?

options.A: Tongue deviation to the right
options.B: Weakness of the left arm and leg
options.C: Right eye turned down and out with ptosis
options.D: Right lateral gaze palsy with right facial weakness
options.E: Hoarseness with a reduced gag reflex on the right

whyNot.A: Tongue deviation comes from the **medial medulla**; his pattern is **lateral** with **full strength**
whyNot.B: **Strength is full**, so there is no corticospinal involvement and no hemiparesis
whyNot.C: A down-and-out eye with ptosis is a **midbrain** (oculomotor) sign, unrelated to his crossed sensory loss
whyNot.D: Gaze palsy with facial weakness is a **pontine** lesion; his deficits are **medullary**

answer: Ipsilateral hoarseness and decreased gag
why: A **lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarct**, usually from PICA or vertebral artery occlusion, damages the spinal trigeminal tract (ipsilateral face), spinothalamic tract (contralateral body) and **nucleus ambiguus**. This gives **ipsilateral hoarseness, dysphagia and reduced gag**.

idea.rule: Lateral medullary syndrome: crossed pain-temperature loss plus nucleus ambiguus signs on the lesion side.
also: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome from descending sympathetic fibers
Ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia from inferior cerebellar peduncle
Nystagmus and vertigo from vestibular nuclei
Vertebral artery dissection is a common cause in the young

stem: A 28-year-old woman had eye pain with blurred vision in one eye last winter that resolved over weeks. This spring she had numbness and heaviness of both legs that also improved. She is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. An MRI of the brain is performed.
oneliner: 28F + recurrent optic and spinal episodes months apart + young woman → which MRI finding?
ask: Which MRI finding is most likely?

options.A: Multiple T2-hyperintense white matter lesions around the ventricles
options.B: Diffuse symmetric white matter change with cerebral atrophy and no discrete lesions
options.C: A solitary ring-enhancing mass next to a ventricle
options.D: Enlarged ventricles out of proportion to cortical sulci
options.E: Symmetric T2 lesion in the central pons

whyNot.B: Diffuse symmetric change with atrophy is seen in **HIV encephalopathy**, a progressive dementia; she has **relapsing-remitting focal episodes** and is otherwise healthy
whyNot.C: A single enhancing mass suggests **lymphoma** or abscess and would not cause separate episodes that **resolve**
whyNot.D: Ventriculomegaly with gait and urinary symptoms is **normal pressure hydrocephalus** in older adults
whyNot.E: Central pontine lesions follow **rapid sodium correction**, and she has had no such event

answer: Multiple periventricular T2-hyperintense plaques
why: Her episodes are **separated in time** and affect **different CNS sites** (optic nerve, then cord or brain), which defines **multiple sclerosis**. MRI shows **periventricular T2/FLAIR plaques**, often oriented perpendicular to the ventricles (**Dawson fingers**).

idea.rule: Multiple sclerosis: multiple periventricular white matter plaques disseminated in space and time.
also: Oligoclonal IgG bands in CSF
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Uhthoff phenomenon: symptoms worsen with heat
Relative afferent pupillary defect after optic neuritis

stem: A 55-year-old man has become rude, impulsive and careless with money over eight months. He makes inappropriate remarks to strangers. His wife says his memory and orientation remain good, and he had no strokes and drinks little alcohol. An MRI is ordered.
oneliner: 55M + months of disinhibition + memory spared + onset in his 50s → which imaging pattern?
ask: Which MRI pattern is most likely?

options.A: Atrophy of the hippocampi and parietal lobes
options.B: Atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes
options.C: Atrophy of the caudate heads with boxcar-shaped ventricles
options.D: Multiple small subcortical infarcts
options.E: Atrophy of the mammillary bodies

whyNot.A: That medial temporal and parietal pattern fits **Alzheimer disease**, which starts with **memory loss**; his memory is **preserved**
whyNot.C: Caudate atrophy goes with **Huntington disease**, which also causes **chorea**
whyNot.D: He has had **no strokes**, and multi-infarct disease gives stepwise deficits rather than pure behavior change with **preserved memory**
whyNot.E: Mammillary body atrophy is a late finding of **thiamine deficiency**, and he **drinks little alcohol**

answer: Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
why: **Frontotemporal dementia** typically begins in the 50s-60s with **personality change and disinhibition** while memory is spared, and **frontal and anterior temporal atrophy** is the characteristic MRI finding. Pick bodies (tau) are seen in the Pick-disease subtype.

idea.rule: Early behavior change with spared memory: frontal and anterior temporal atrophy (FTD).
also: Pick bodies are round tau-positive inclusions
Primary progressive aphasia is a language-variant presentation
Alzheimer disease causes hippocampal and parietal atrophy
Frontal release signs

stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV has not taken antiretroviral therapy for years; his CD4 count is 45/mm3. Over several months his family has noticed slowed thinking, apathy and forgetfulness. He is afebrile with no headache, no seizures and no focal weakness. An MRI is performed.
oneliner: 40M + untreated HIV + low CD4 + slowing and apathy + no focal signs or fever → which MRI finding?
ask: Which MRI finding is most likely?

options.A: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction
options.B: A solitary enhancing periventricular mass
options.C: Asymmetric non-enhancing white matter lesions, no atrophy
options.D: Symmetric white matter hyperintensity with atrophy, no enhancement
options.E: Enhancement of the basal meninges

whyNot.A: Ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS point to **toxoplasmosis**, which usually causes **fever, headache or focal signs**; he has none
whyNot.B: A solitary enhancing mass is classical for **lymphoma** and would typically cause **focal deficits or mass effect**
whyNot.C: Asymmetric non-enhancing lesions without atrophy suggest **PML**, which causes **focal neurologic deficits**; he has none
whyNot.E: Basal meningeal enhancement fits **cryptococcal or tubercular meningitis**, which causes **fever and headache**

answer: Diffuse symmetric white matter change with atrophy
why: **HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder** is a subcortical dementia driven by HIV-infected microglia and macrophages in the brain. MRI shows **diffuse, symmetric white matter hyperintensity with atrophy** and **no mass effect or contrast enhancement**, in a patient with advanced untreated disease.

idea.rule: Untreated advanced HIV with slowing and apathy: symmetric white matter change and atrophy, no mass or enhancement.
also: Improves with antiretroviral therapy
Microglial nodules with multinucleated giant cells are the histologic hallmark
Subcortical dementia: slowing and apathy early, cortical signs late
PML is JC virus with asymmetric demyelination

stem: A 72-year-old woman dies of pneumonia. Years earlier a fall caused a complete thoracic spinal cord injury. A myelin stain of her cervical cord shows pallor of the medial portion of the dorsal columns, and the lateral portion looks normal.
oneliner: 72F + old thoracic cord injury + pale medial dorsal column in the cervical cord → which symptom was present?
ask: Which finding was most likely present in life?

options.A: Loss of vibration sense in both hands
options.B: Absent knee reflexes
options.C: Loss of vibration and position sense in both feet
options.D: Brisk triceps reflexes
options.E: Atrophy of the arm muscles

whyNot.A: Hand fibers run in the **lateral** dorsal column (cuneate), which is **normal** on her stain
whyNot.B: The L2-L4 reflex arc lies **below the thoracic injury** and loses descending inhibition, so knee jerks become brisk, not absent; the pallor is also **sensory**
whyNot.D: Her upper-limb pathways and arm reflexes are **above the injury and intact**
whyNot.E: Arm muscle wasting would need cervical anterior horn damage; her **cervical cord is normal** apart from tract degeneration

answer: Loss of vibration and position sense in the feet
why: Leg fibers (from below T6) ascend in the **medial dorsal column, the fasciculus gracilis**. After the thoracic injury these axons degenerate upward, producing **medial dorsal column pallor** in the cervical cord. The deficit during life was therefore **loss of vibration and proprioception in both legs and feet**.

idea.rule: Fasciculus gracilis carries leg vibration and position sense; fasciculus cuneatus (lateral) carries arm input.
also: Tabes dorsalis and vitamin B12 deficiency also damage dorsal columns
Positive Romberg sign
Dorsal column fibers cross in the medulla (medial lemniscus)
Ascending tracts degenerate above a cord lesion; descending corticospinal fibers degenerate below it

stem: A 24-year-old woman has been on a ventilator for three weeks after a barbiturate overdose caused a prolonged cardiac arrest. Her eyes now open at times. On repeated testing she never follows commands or tracks a person, even by blinking, and she coughs when suctioned. She breathes over the ventilator rate.
oneliner: 24F + 3 weeks after anoxic coma + eyes open + no command-following or tracking + cough on suction → which finding set fits?
ask: Which set of findings fits her state?

options.A: Sleep-wake cycles and brainstem reflexes intact, no purposeful response
options.B: Absent brainstem reflexes and no spontaneous breathing
options.C: Fully aware, with only vertical gaze and blinking preserved
options.D: Eyes closed throughout, no sleep-wake cycles, brainstem reflexes intact
options.E: Eyes open with inconsistent but reproducible command-following

whyNot.B: She **coughs on suction and breathes over the ventilator**, so brainstem function is intact, which excludes brain death
whyNot.C: Locked-in patients are aware and **blink to command**; she **never responds even by blinking**
whyNot.D: Her **eyes open at times**, which means she has moved beyond coma
whyNot.E: She **never follows commands, even inconsistently**, which excludes the minimally conscious state

answer: Vegetative state (wakefulness without awareness)
why: After diffuse cortical injury the brainstem recovers and the patient regains **sleep-wake cycles with open eyes**, but shows **no awareness or purposeful response** (called persistent once it lasts about a month). **Brainstem reflexes and respiration are intact** and the EEG is diffusely slow.

idea.rule: Vegetative state: wakefulness without awareness; brainstem reflexes intact, cortex severely damaged.
also: Brain death: loss of all brain activity including brainstem; apnea test positive
Locked-in syndrome: ventral pontine lesion, awareness preserved
Minimally conscious state: inconsistent but reproducible purposeful behavior
Coma: no eye opening and no sleep-wake cycles

stem: An 8-year-old girl is sent by her teacher because she stops mid-sentence and stares blankly many times a day for several seconds, then carries on as if nothing happened. She is alert immediately afterward. Blowing on a pinwheel for three minutes provokes an episode in the office.
oneliner: 8F + daily brief staring spells + no confusion afterward + provoked by hyperventilation → which EEG/feature fits?
ask: Which EEG finding is most likely?

options.A: Sharp waves over the anterior temporal region
options.B: Chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal spikes
options.C: Generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges
options.D: Periodic sharp wave complexes
options.E: Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges

whyNot.A: Focal temporal sharp waves suit **focal impaired-awareness seizures**, which cause **minutes of postictal confusion**; she recovers at once
whyNot.B: That pattern (**hypsarrhythmia**) belongs to **infantile spasms** in babies, not a school-age child with staring
whyNot.C: Polyspike-wave with myoclonic jerks suits **juvenile myoclonic epilepsy** in adolescents; she has **no jerks**
whyNot.D: Periodic complexes go with **prion disease** and rapidly progressive dementia

answer: Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave
why: Brief staring with **abrupt onset and offset, no aura and no postictal state**, provoked by **hyperventilation**, is typical of **absence seizures**. The EEG shows **generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave** discharges from thalamocortical oscillation.

idea.rule: Absence seizures: brief unresponsive stares, no postictal state, 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG.
also: First-line treatment is ethosuximide, which blocks T-type calcium channels
Valproate covers absence plus tonic-clonic seizures
Hyperventilation provokes absence seizures in most untreated children
Focal impaired-awareness seizures have automatisms and postictal confusion

stem: A 70-year-old man has an acute infarct of the left posterior temporal lobe. Afterward he talks easily and at a normal pace, yet his replies to questions do not match what was asked and he cannot carry out a simple instruction. He appears cheerful and unconcerned.
oneliner: 70M + left posterior temporal stroke + talks easily but replies mismatch questions → which language finding set?
ask: Which set of language findings fits?

options.A: Halting, effortful speech, intact comprehension
options.B: Fluent paraphasic speech, poor comprehension and repetition
options.C: Fluent speech, intact comprehension, poor repetition
options.D: Nonfluent speech, intact comprehension and repetition
options.E: Mute with poor comprehension

whyNot.A: Effortful speech with intact comprehension is **Broca** aphasia; he speaks **easily** and **cannot follow instructions**
whyNot.C: Intact comprehension with poor repetition is **conduction** aphasia, but he **cannot follow a simple instruction**
whyNot.D: His speech is **fluent**, not nonfluent
whyNot.E: He **talks easily**, so he is not mute

answer: Fluent paraphasic speech with poor comprehension and repetition (Wernicke aphasia)
why: The **superior temporal gyrus** (Wernicke area) handles comprehension. A lesion there gives **fluent speech with paraphasias and empty content**, **poor comprehension and poor repetition**, and little awareness of the problem, so patients are not frustrated.

idea.rule: Wernicke aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension and repetition, unaware.
also: Usually an inferior-division left MCA stroke
Broca aphasia: nonfluent with intact comprehension, frontal lesion
Conduction aphasia: arcuate fasciculus lesion, poor repetition only
Associated right superior visual field deficit from temporal optic radiation involvement

stem: A 54-year-old woman has seemed puzzled by ordinary things at home for two days. MRI shows an acute infarct of the left occipital and inferior temporal cortex; the thalamus and frontal and parietal lobes are spared.
oneliner: 54F + 2 days puzzled at home + acute left occipitotemporal infarct, thalamus spared → which deficit is expected?
ask: Which deficit is most likely?

options.A: Right leg weaker than right arm
options.B: Fluent speech with poor comprehension
options.C: Pure right face, arm and leg weakness
options.D: Cannot name objects by sight but can by touch
options.E: Loss of all sensation on the right side

whyNot.A: Leg-predominant weakness comes from the **ACA** territory of the medial frontal and parietal lobes, which are **spared**
whyNot.B: Wernicke aphasia needs the **superior temporal gyrus** (MCA); her infarct is **occipital and inferior temporal**
whyNot.C: A pure motor syndrome is a **lacunar internal capsule** infarct, outside her **occipitotemporal** lesion
whyNot.E: Hemisensory loss of all modalities needs the **thalamus** (PCA perforators), which is **spared**

answer: Visual object agnosia
why: The **PCA** supplies the occipital lobe and inferior temporal cortex. Damage to the **occipitotemporal association cortex** causes **visual agnosia**: objects are not recognized by sight, but identification by touch or sound remains intact. Prosopagnosia arises in the same territory.

idea.rule: PCA infarct: visual deficits (hemianopia, agnosia, alexia), with motor and sensory function spared.
also: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Prosopagnosia from fusiform gyrus lesions
Alexia without agraphia from splenium involvement
Thalamic infarcts arise from PCA thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate branches

stem: A 58-year-old man has a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing since a left carotid endarterectomy. Liquids sometimes come out of his nose. When he says "ah", the soft palate rises poorly on the left.
oneliner: 58M + hoarse + dysphagia + nasal regurgitation after left carotid surgery + left palate lags → uvula position?
ask: Which of the following uvula findings is most likely?

options.A: Deviation to the left, toward the side of the lesion
options.B: No deviation at rest or on saying "ah"
options.C: Deviation to the left at rest only
options.D: Deviation to the right, away from the lesion
options.E: Deviation to the left only during swallowing

whyNot.A: The weak left side cannot pull the uvula, so it is **pulled toward the strong right side**; deviation to the lesion is the tongue pattern
whyNot.B: A palate that rises poorly on one side **gives an asymmetric pull**, so the uvula will not sit midline on phonation
whyNot.C: The uvula is judged **on saying "ah"**, when the strong right side contracts and pulls it rightward, not leftward
whyNot.E: Deviation on swallowing only is not the vagal finding; the **test is saying "ah"**, where the weak side lags

answer: Deviation to the right, away from the lesion
why: Hoarseness, dysphagia and nasal regurgitation with a lagging left palate indicate a **left vagus (CN X) lesion**. The intact right side contracts and **pulls the uvula toward itself**, so it deviates **away from the lesion**.

idea.rule: With a vagal lesion the uvula points away from the weak side; the tongue points toward the weak side.
also: Tongue deviates toward the side of a hypoglossal lesion
Jaw deviates toward the side of a trigeminal motor lesion
Palate lags on the side of the vagal lesion
